extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists who write and check nontrivial proofs (including those interested in mechanized/formal verification)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing hierarchical, explicitly scoped proofs (Lamport's 21st‑century style / TLA+ proof primitives) so proofs are checkable, avoid common informal errors, and can be translated to machine-checked proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical numbering / explicit step numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof at level n is decomposed into sub-proofs at level n+1, with explicit numbering (e.g. ⟨1⟩1, ⟨1⟩2, ...). Each step has a fixed reference so later steps can cite it precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit hierarchical numbering so every step has a permanent address; enforce a variable‑scoping discipline (sub-proofs cannot reference results from sibling sub-proofs at deeper levels). This makes scope violations mechanically checkable and prevents ambiguity about which statements are being cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASSUME / PROVE at each step
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly declare the hypotheses in scope and the goal at each step using ASSUME/PROVE (instead of vague prose like "now we want to show...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clearly what is assumed and exactly what is to be proved at every level so readers (and tools) know the local context; eliminates prose ambiguity about the current objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEW: explicit introduction of variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce new variables explicitly (NEW) with stated type/conditions rather than implicitly in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a variable is introduced, name it and state its properties. Avoid implicit introductions which lead to scope and quantifier confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: SUFFICES: document and justify reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reducing the current goal to another statement, state that proving statement A would suffice to prove the current goal (SUFFICES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make reductions explicit and correct: if you claim SUFFICES A, ensure A indeed implies the goal. Incorrect SUFFICES steps produce vacuous or wrong proofs; check that the reduction preserves meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: PICK: name witnesses when choosing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof selects an element from a set, use PICK to choose and explicitly name the witness and state its properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For existential arguments, name the chosen element and record why it satisfies required properties; avoid vague "choose x" prose that leaves witness properties implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASE: explicit case decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use explicit CASE markers to structure case-by-case reasoning instead of informal enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate all cases explicitly. The hierarchical CASE structure helps prevent forgotten cases and makes it clear which subproof addresses which branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: QED / explicit end-of-proof markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark proof completion at each level (QED) to indicate that the goal at that level has been achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit termination markers to avoid ambiguity about whether a step or subproof is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical checkability and machine-checkable structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure proofs so a reader (or checker) can mechanically verify each step without reconstructing lost context; ideally the structure is machine-checkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the proof so it can, in principle, be translated straightforwardly into a formal proof script (Lean/Coq/Isabelle/TLA+). Avoid prose that requires significant reconstruction to formalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forgotten cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure case enumerations are complete; do not rely on informal WLOG/symmetry claims that may hide missing branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list and handle every case. Warnings: prose often omits cases silently; the hierarchical CASE discipline helps catch omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid quantifier-scope confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Make quantifier scopes explicit; do not introduce or use variables outside their declared scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NEW and ASSUME/PROVE to control scope. Quantifier-order and scope errors are common in prose proofs; explicit scoping prevents these mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hidden hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Every step must state which hypotheses are in scope; do not rely on implicit assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a step depends on an assumption, that assumption must appear in the local ASSUME list. The 'curious‑child' test (ask 'Why?') helps reveal hidden premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the conclusion (or consequences of it) to justify a sub-step of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explicit hierarchical structure and scoping make circular dependencies visible; check dependency graph to ensure acyclicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vacuous or incorrect reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure SUFFICES steps and other reductions actually reduce the problem correctly rather than proving an irrelevant or weaker statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that the chosen reduction implies the original goal and that no hidden conditions make the reduction vacuous. Lamport highlights 'vacuous reductions' as an error class caught by structured proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit handling of routine or inductive steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not sweep routine details (e.g. induction base/step checks) under informal phrases like 'by induction' without checking the induction's correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out induction hypotheses, base cases, and the mechanism by which the step follows; structured proofs force verification of routine steps that prose often glosses over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize use of 'WLOG', 'clearly', and similar shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using shorthand dismissals that skip justification ('WLOG', 'clearly', etc.), because they often hide missing arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If symmetry or a reduction is used, justify why the omitted cases follow; explicit CASE or SUFFICES structure should be used instead of informal shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curious‑child principle
rubrics_metrics.description: After every assertion imagine a curious child asking 'Why?'; if you cannot answer at the next level, the proof is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a test: every claim must be justified by the immediately lower‑level steps. The technique encourages completeness and surfacing hidden steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑confirmation‑bias principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain suspicion of your own beliefs and externalize verification to avoid overlooking gaps that support your preferred conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured proofs reduce the writer's ability to gloss over problems; the method explicitly forces inspection of assumptions and reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When prose proofs are acceptable (exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, conceptually deep 'magic' proofs may be better left in concise prose; structured form can be excessive for one-page insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply structured proofs especially for long proofs, algorithm proofs with many invariants, proofs with subtle quantifier order, and proofs intended for verification. Use discretion: brevity and insight can justify prose in small-scale, truly elementary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs should be translatable to formal proof systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer structures and conventions that make translation to formal systems (Lean, Coq, Isabelle, TLA+) straightforward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof that follows Lamport's primitives and hierarchical discipline is often much easier to convert into a machine‑checked proof than a prose proof; treat machine-compatibility as a quality objective when appropriate.
